draft.title: One-tail and two-tail tests
card: One-tail test
The alternative hypothesis names one direction only: H₁: μ > 50 or H₁: μ < 50. Use it when the question asks about an increase only, or a decrease only.
Two-tail test
The alternative hypothesis allows a change either way: H₁: μ ≠ 50. Use it when the question asks whether the mean has changed, with no direction given.
The p-value is the probability of a result at least as extreme as the sample result. In a two-tail test, extreme means far from μ in either direction, so you count both tails.
For a symmetric distribution such as the normal, the two-tail p-value is double the one-tail p-value. Example: if P(Z > 1.5) = 0.067, the two-tail p-value is 2 × 0.067 = 0.134.
draft.remember: The wording of H₁ sets the tails. A two-tail p-value doubles the one-tail value.

a.q: A tyre maker claims its tyres last 40 000 km on average. A tester wants to know if the mean differs from this. Which H₁ is used?
a.why: The tester asks if the mean differs, with no direction given, so the alternative allows a change either way: μ ≠ 40 000. The option μ = 40 000 is wrong because it is the null hypothesis, not the alternative.
a.clue: No direction is mentioned in the question.

b.q: A test of H₀: μ = 12 against H₁: μ > 12 gives a one-tail p-value of 0.03. The same data is used for H₁: μ ≠ 12. What is the two-tail p-value?
b.why: Both tails are counted in a two-tail test, and the normal distribution is symmetric, so the p-value doubles: 2 × 0.03 = 0.06. Halving to 0.015 is the tempting mistake, and it goes the wrong way because two tails hold more probability than one.
b.clue: A two-tail test counts extreme results in both directions.

problems.detail: The remember line says flatly that a two-tail p-value doubles the one-tail value. The card limits this to symmetric distributions such as the normal, and it also only holds when the sample result lies in the direction of H₁. The remember line states the rule more broadly than the card does.

The card defines the p-value ('the probability of a result at least as extreme as the sample result'). That term belongs to point 5 (p-values and significance), so it should only be mentioned here, not defined.
The p-value definition leaves out the condition 'assuming the null hypothesis is true'. Without it, a student could take the p-value as an unconditional probability.

final.title: One-tail and two-tail tests
card: One-tail test
The alternative hypothesis names one direction only: \(H_{1}: \mu > 50\) or \(H_{1}: \mu < 50\). Use it when the question asks about an increase only, or a decrease only.
Two-tail test
The alternative hypothesis allows a change either way: \(H_{1}: \mu \ne 50\). Use it when the question asks whether the mean has changed, with no direction given.
A one-tail test counts extreme results only in the tail named by \(H_{1}\). A two-tail test counts results far from the null mean in either direction, so its p-value uses both tails.

For a symmetric distribution such as the normal, when the sample result lies on the side named in \(H_{1}\), the two-tail p-value is double the one-tail p-value. Example: if \(\text{Pr}(Z > 1.5) = 0.067\), the two-tail p-value is \(2 \times 0.067 = 0.134\).

4.alt: The standard normal curve for \(Z\). Both tails are shaded: to the left of \(-1.5\) and to the right of 1.5, each with area 0.067. For a two-tail test the p-value uses both, \(2 \times 0.067 = 0.134\).

final.remember: The wording of \(H_{1}\) sets the tails. One tail looks one way, two tails look both ways.

a.q: A tyre maker claims its tyres last 40 000 km on average. A tester wants to know if the mean differs from this. Which \(H_{1}\) is used?
a.why: The tester asks if the mean differs, with no direction given, so the alternative allows a change either way: \(\mu \ne 40\,000\). The option \(\mu = 40\,000\) is wrong because it is the null hypothesis, not the alternative.
a.clue: No direction is mentioned in the question.

b.q: A test of \(H_{0}: \mu = 12\) against \(H_{1}: \mu > 12\) uses a normal distribution and gives a one-tail p-value of 0.03. The same data is used for \(H_{1}: \mu \ne 12\). What is the two-tail p-value?
b.why: A one-tail p-value of 0.03 means the sample mean lies above 12, on the side named in \(H_{1}\). The normal is symmetric, so counting both tails doubles it: \(2 \times 0.03 = 0.06\). Halving to 0.015 goes the wrong way, because two tails hold more probability than one.
b.clue: A two-tail test counts extreme results in both directions.
